column1: How Major Policy Decisions Are Taken

column2: Decision-Making Process: Major policy decisions involve several authorities and stages
Example – Office Memorandum 1990: Decision to reserve 27% jobs for SEBC after a long process
Key Steps

column3: Mandal Commission Report (1980): Recommended reservation for SEBC
President’s Address: Announced government’s intention in Parliament
Union Cabinet Decision: Took formal approval to implement the policy
Prime Minister’s Statement: Informed both Houses of Parliament
Final Order Issued: Department of Personnel and Training drafted and signed the order

column2: Dispute Resolution

column3: Supreme Court Judgment (1992): Upheld the order but excluded the creamy layer

column2: Definition of Institutions: Arrangements to perform key democratic functions
Purpose

column3: Governance Tasks: Security, welfare, education, taxation, and administration
Value of Delays: Ensure consultation and prevent hasty or wrong decisions

column2: Role and Powers

column3: Legislative Authority: Makes, amends, or abolishes laws
Government Control: Government functions only with Parliament’s support
Financial Control: No public money can be spent without Parliament’s approval
Forum of Debate: Highest platform for national discussion

column2: Two Houses of Parliament

column3: Lok Sabha (House of the People)

column4: Elected Directly: Members chosen by the people
Greater Powers: Final authority in joint sessions
Money Bills Control: Rajya Sabha can delay money bills for only 14 days
Control over Executive: Can remove Council of Ministers through no-confidence motion

column3: Rajya Sabha (Council of States)

column4: Indirectly Elected: Represents states and regions
Federal Role: Protects interests of states

column2: Political Executive

column3: Elected Leaders: Ministers elected for a fixed term
Policy Decisions: Take major decisions and are answerable to people

column2: Permanent Executive

column3: Civil Servants: Appointed on a long-term basis
Administrative Role: Implement decisions and manage daily administration

column2: Why Political Executive is More Powerful

column3: Democratic Principle: Elected representatives reflect people’s will

column2: Head of Government: Exercises real executive authority
Cabinet Leadership: Chairs Cabinet meetings and resolves inter-departmental disputes
Ministerial Oversight: Distributes work and can dismiss ministers
Collective Responsibility: Resignation of PM leads to resignation of entire ministry
Coalition Constraints: Must accommodate alliance partners in coalition governments
Head of State: Performs nominal and ceremonial functions
Supervisory Role: Ensures coordination among political institutions
Executive Authority: All laws and major decisions issued in President’s name
Major Appointments: Appoints judges, governors, and election commissioners
Military and Legislative Role

column3: Supreme Commander: Head of the defence forces
Assent to Bills: Law comes into force only after President’s approval

column2: Discretionary Power: Appoints Prime Minister when no clear majority exists
Integrated Judiciary: Supreme Court controls judicial system nationwide
Judicial Independence

column3: Separation of Powers: Free from executive and legislative control
Impeachment Procedure: Judges removed only by special majority in Parliament

column2: Judicial Review: Power to check constitutionality of laws and executive actions
Guardian of Fundamental Rights

column3: Public Interest Litigation: Citizens can approach courts to protect public interest
